body:
Why does food need preservation?

Fresh food does not remain suitable for consumption indefinitely. Milk may turn sour, bread may develop mould, fruits may rot, and oil-rich foods may develop an unpleasant smell. These changes occur because of microorganisms, chemical reactions, and natural enzymes present in food.

Food preservation is the use of suitable methods to prevent or delay food spoilage and maintain food safety and quality for a longer period.

Preservation is important because it reduces food wastage, permits seasonal foods to be stored, makes transportation easier, and helps maintain a supply of food between production and consumption.

The main causes of food spoilage

1. Growth of microorganisms

Bacteria, yeasts and moulds are microorganisms associated with many forms of food spoilage. Their growth depends on factors such as available moisture, temperature, nutrients and the chemical conditions of the food. Different microorganisms have different requirements.

Moist bread kept in a warm place may develop fungal growth. Milk may become sour because microorganisms produce acids. Certain microorganisms can also produce harmful substances in food, causing food poisoning.

Not all microorganisms are harmful. Selected microorganisms are deliberately used to prepare curd, bread and other fermented foods. The important distinction is between controlled activity by useful microorganisms and unwanted microbial contamination or growth.

2. Oxidation and rancidity

Oxygen in air can react with substances present in food. When fats and oils undergo oxidation, their smell and taste may deteriorate. This is called rancidity.

For example, an opened packet of fried snacks may gradually develop an unpleasant smell because its fats react with oxygen. Rancidity is primarily a chemical change. It should not be confused with the growth of mould or bacteria, although both types of deterioration may occur in the same food.

3. Enzymatic changes

Food contains natural substances called enzymes, which help chemical reactions occur. Some enzymes can cause changes in colour, flavour or texture after harvesting or cutting. The browning of a freshly cut apple is a familiar example of an oxidation-related enzymatic change.

Thus, spoilage is not always caused by microorganisms alone.

The basic principles of preservation

Most preservation methods work by controlling one or more conditions responsible for deterioration:

  • Reducing microorganisms: Heating can destroy many microorganisms, while hygienic handling reduces contamination.
  • Slowing microbial growth: Refrigeration, drying, salting, sugaring and acidification make conditions less favourable for many microbes.
  • Limiting oxygen exposure: Airtight packaging, vacuum packaging and nitrogen flushing can slow oxidation and the growth of organisms that require oxygen.
  • Preventing recontamination: Clean, suitable containers and proper storage protect food after preparation or processing.

Several methods are often used together. For example, properly prepared pickles may rely on salt, acid, reduced moisture availability and suitable storage conditions rather than on a single ingredient.

Food quality and food safety are different

Spoiled food may have a changed colour, smell or taste. However, food containing harmful microorganisms or their toxins does not always show an obvious change. A pleasant smell or normal appearance does not prove that food is safe.

Prelims focus

  • Food preservation delays spoilage and helps maintain food safety and quality.
  • Bacteria, yeasts and moulds can cause food spoilage.
  • Rancidity is associated with oxidation of fats and oils.
  • Useful microorganisms are employed in controlled fermentation.
  • Trap: Food spoilage is not always microbial; oxidation and enzymatic changes also occur.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 2, Microorganisms: Friend and Foe, sections 2.3–2.5, printed pp. 19–26; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 1, Chemical Reactions and Equations, section 1.3.2, Rancidity, printed p. 13.]

title: Why Food Spoils and How Food Preservation Works

body:
Preservation by heat

Heat is used to destroy or reduce microorganisms that can cause spoilage or disease. Its effectiveness depends on the temperature reached, the duration of heating and the type of microorganism.

Boiling

Boiling milk or other suitable foods destroys many harmful microorganisms. It is a familiar household method of making food safer and delaying spoilage.

However, boiling does not necessarily destroy every resistant microbial spore. Boiled food can also become contaminated again during handling or storage. Therefore, boiling should not be understood as a guarantee of indefinite preservation.

Pasteurisation of milk

Pasteurisation is a controlled heat treatment that reduces harmful microorganisms in a food or beverage while avoiding the more severe heating associated with sterilisation.

Pasteurisation is especially important for milk. Two commonly recognised milk-pasteurisation methods are:

  • Batch or low-temperature, long-time treatment: Heating milk to at least 63°C for 30 minutes.
  • High-temperature, short-time treatment: Heating milk to at least 72°C for 15 seconds.

After pasteurisation, milk is rapidly cooled. Food Safety and Standards Authority of India guidance for milk processing specifies immediate cooling to 4°C or lower after pasteurisation. Proper packaging and continued refrigeration help prevent subsequent microbial growth.

The process is associated with Louis Pasteur, whose work helped establish the scientific importance of microorganisms in fermentation and spoilage.

Pasteurisation and UHT treatment are not identical

Ultra-high-temperature treatment, commonly abbreviated as UHT, uses much higher temperatures for a very short time. One commonly used treatment is approximately 135°C for 1–2 seconds.

When UHT-treated milk is filled into suitable sterile packaging under aseptic conditions, the unopened package can be stored without refrigeration for the period specified by the manufacturer. Ordinary pasteurised milk, by contrast, generally requires refrigeration even before opening.

After opening either type of package, the milk can be contaminated by its surroundings and should be stored according to the label instructions.

Preservation by low temperature

Refrigeration

Refrigeration slows the growth of many microorganisms and reduces the rate of several chemical and enzymatic reactions. It therefore extends the usable life of many foods, including milk, cooked dishes and fresh vegetables.

Refrigeration does not sterilise food. Some microorganisms can grow slowly even at refrigerator temperatures. Food should not be kept indefinitely merely because it is refrigerated.

Freezing

Freezing converts much of the water in food into ice. The resulting low temperature and reduced availability of liquid water greatly restrict microbial growth and slow chemical changes.

However, freezing does not reliably destroy all microorganisms. Some remain alive and can become active again after thawing. Consequently, thawed food requires suitable handling and storage.

Preservation by drying

Microorganisms need available water to grow. Drying removes moisture and makes food less favourable for microbial activity.

Common examples include dried chillies, grains, spices, dried fruits and certain dried fish products. Sun drying is a traditional method, while controlled drying is also widely used in food processing.

The scientific principle is the reduction of available water, not necessarily the complete removal of every water molecule. Even dried foods can spoil if they absorb moisture from humid air or are stored unhygienically.

Comparison of the main methods

MethodMain principleImportant limitation
BoilingDestroys many microorganisms through heatDoes not guarantee destruction of all spores
PasteurisationControlled reduction of harmful microbesUsually requires continued cold storage
RefrigerationSlows microbial growthDoes not sterilise food
FreezingStrongly restricts microbial activitySurviving microbes may become active after thawing
DryingReduces available moistureMoisture absorption can permit renewed spoilage

Prelims focus

  • Batch pasteurisation of milk: 63°C for 30 minutes.
  • High-temperature, short-time pasteurisation: 72°C for 15 seconds.
  • FSSAI milk-processing guidance specifies cooling pasteurised milk to 4°C or lower.
  • Refrigeration slows microbial growth; it does not kill all microorganisms.
  • Drying preserves food mainly by reducing available water.
  • Trap: Properly aseptically packed UHT milk and ordinary pasteurised milk do not have the same unopened storage requirements.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 2, Microorganisms: Friend and Foe, section 2.5, Food Preservation, printed p. 26; Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, Milk and Milk Product Processing, Food Safety Inspection Checklist, items 23–24, 2020, consulted 3 November 2026; Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011, section 2.1.1, milk and pasteurisation provisions, consolidated version dated 31 January 2022.]

pictures.alt: Either milk heat treatment is followed by rapid cooling, hygienic packaging and refrigeration; some spores may survive.
pictures.caption: Pasteurisation combines controlled heating with rapid cooling.

title: Food Preservation by Heating, Cooling and Drying

body:
How ordinary substances help preserve food

Several familiar kitchen ingredients can delay spoilage by making the food environment less suitable for microorganisms. Salt and sugar mainly reduce the availability of water. Vinegar increases acidity. Oil can provide a barrier against exposure to air and contamination when used as part of a properly prepared product.

These methods are especially familiar in the preparation of pickles, jams, jellies and preserved fruits.

Preservation by common salt

Common salt is sodium chloride. When present at a sufficiently high concentration, salt reduces the availability of water to microorganisms. Water may move out of microbial cells through osmosis, making growth difficult for many species.

Salting has traditionally been used to preserve fish, meat, amla, raw mangoes and other foods.

The effect depends on the amount of salt, the type of food, its moisture content and the organisms present. A small quantity of salt added merely for taste is not necessarily enough to preserve a food.

Preservation by sugar

Concentrated sugar has a similar overall effect on water availability. It binds part of the water present in food, making less water available for the growth of many spoilage microorganisms.

This principle is used in jams, jellies and certain fruit preserves. Their relatively high sugar content helps slow spoilage when combined with appropriate preparation, acidity, packaging and storage.

A lightly sweetened drink does not become safely preserved simply because sugar has been added. Preservation depends on adequate concentration and the other conditions of the product.

Preservation by vinegar and acidity

Vinegar contains acetic acid. Adding sufficient food-grade acid lowers the pH of a food, making conditions unfavourable for many microorganisms.

Acidification is useful in several types of pickle. However, adding an arbitrary quantity of vinegar does not establish that a product is safe for long storage. The final acidity throughout the food is important.

Use of a tested preservation method is important for stored pickles. Low-acid, moisture-rich foods can remain unsafe even when they appear to be covered by vinegar or oil.

Preservation by edible oil

Oil is commonly used in Indian pickles. A layer of oil can reduce direct exposure of the food surface to air and help limit some forms of contamination.

However, oil alone is not a reliable method of destroying harmful microorganisms. Some dangerous microorganisms can grow in low-oxygen conditions if sufficient moisture and other favourable conditions are present. Oil is therefore best understood as one component of a properly prepared preservation system, not as a universal preservative.

Chemical food preservatives

Some substances added to foods are specifically intended to inhibit spoilage. Examples named in school-level science are:

  • Sodium benzoate: Used in suitable acidic food products, including certain beverages and fruit preparations.
  • Sodium metabisulphite: Used in certain permitted food applications to limit spoilage and undesirable changes.

Such additives must be used only in permitted foods and within applicable food-safety requirements. Their usefulness does not mean that unlimited quantities are safe.

PreservativeMain actionTypical application
SaltReduces available waterSalted fish, amla and some pickles
SugarReduces available water at sufficient concentrationJam and jelly
VinegarIncreases acidityAcidified pickles
Edible oilLimits exposure to air and some contaminationPrepared pickles
Approved chemical preservativesInhibit specified spoilage processesPermitted fruit products and beverages

Why several preservation methods may be combined

A properly prepared mango pickle illustrates the combined use of preservation methods. Salt can restrict microbial growth by reducing available water. Adequate acidity can make the food less favourable to many harmful microorganisms. Oil may help reduce exposure to air and contamination. Hygienic preparation and appropriate storage remain necessary.

Prelims focus

  • Salt and concentrated sugar preserve food chiefly by reducing available water.
  • Vinegar contains acetic acid and preserves suitable foods by increasing acidity.
  • Oil is commonly used in pickles but does not itself sterilise food.
  • Sodium benzoate and sodium metabisulphite are named chemical food preservatives.
  • Trap: Adding a little salt or sugar for flavour is not equivalent to preserving food with a sufficiently concentrated solution.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 2, Microorganisms: Friend and Foe, section 2.5, Food Preservation, printed p. 26; National Center for Home Food Preservation, General Information on Fermenting, sections on ingredients, pickles and prevention of spoilage, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Mango pickle needs salt, acidity, an oil layer, hygienic preparation and suitable storage together; oil alone does not sterilise food.
pictures.caption: Multiple protective conditions can act together in a pickle.

title: Preservation Using Salt, Sugar, Vinegar, Oil and Food Preservatives

body:
Why the air inside a food package matters

Air contains oxygen. Oxygen can support the growth of microorganisms that require it and can react with fats and oils, causing rancidity.

Food packaging can help limit contact with external air and prevent dust, insects and other contaminants from reaching the food. However, different packaging methods act in different ways.

Airtight packaging

An airtight container is designed to prevent significant exchange of air between the inside and outside. It may still contain ordinary air when first sealed.

For example, dry biscuits stored in a tightly closed container are protected against moisture and contamination from the surroundings. The airtight seal does not necessarily remove the oxygen already present inside.

Vacuum packaging

Vacuum packaging is a method in which most of the air is removed from a suitable package before it is sealed.

Removing air reduces oxygen exposure. This can slow the oxidation of fats and reduce the growth of some microorganisms that require oxygen. It can also help protect appropriately dried foods from deterioration during storage.

The term vacuum does not mean that the food becomes completely free from all gases or microorganisms.

What vacuum packaging cannot do

Vacuum packaging is not the same as sterilisation. It does not reliably kill bacteria, destroy existing toxins or make unsafe food safe.

Removing oxygen can also favour certain microorganisms that grow in low-oxygen conditions. For example, Clostridium botulinum can grow and produce a dangerous toxin under suitable low-oxygen conditions.

Therefore, a moist perishable food that required refrigeration before vacuum packaging generally still requires refrigeration or freezing afterward. A vacuum seal by itself does not make such food safe for storage at room temperature.

A swollen or damaged package must not be treated as safe merely because it was originally vacuum packed. Packaging cannot replace suitable food processing, temperature control and hygiene.

Nitrogen flushing

Packets of fried snacks are often filled with nitrogen gas before sealing. Nitrogen is comparatively unreactive under ordinary food-storage conditions. It replaces much of the oxygen that would otherwise remain around the food.

This slows oxidation of the fats present in the snacks and thereby delays rancidity. The gas-filled space also helps protect fragile snack pieces from crushing.

Nitrogen flushing is not the same process as vacuum packaging:

  • In vacuum packaging, air is removed before sealing.
  • In nitrogen flushing, much of the air is displaced by nitrogen.
  • In ordinary airtight packaging, the existing air may remain trapped inside the container.

Why packaging is often combined with another treatment

For a dry food, reduced moisture and good packaging may together extend storage life. For a refrigerated food, suitable packaging and low temperature work together. For commercially heat-processed foods, the required heat treatment and the integrity of the package are both important.

Thus, the usefulness of a packaging method depends on the nature of the food, its previous treatment and its intended storage conditions.

Prelims focus

  • Vacuum packaging removes most air before sealing.
  • Limiting oxygen exposure can slow rancidity.
  • Nitrogen flushing replaces oxygen-rich air rather than creating a vacuum.
  • Nitrogen is used in packages of oil-rich snacks to reduce oxidation.
  • Vacuum packing does not sterilise food.
  • Trap: Vacuum-packed perishable food is not automatically safe for unrefrigerated storage.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 1, Chemical Reactions and Equations, section 1.3.2, Rancidity, printed p. 13; Utah State University Extension, Packaging Foods, section Vacuum Package Foods, consulted 3 November 2026; World Health Organization, Botulism, sections on causes and foodborne botulism, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Two workers vacuum-pack dried fruit and nuts in transparent pouches and stack sealed packets in a clean Indian food-packing workplace.
pictures.caption: Food packaging can reduce exposure to air and contamination.

pictures.alt: Airtight sealing can retain air; vacuum removes most air; nitrogen replaces air. Lower oxygen slows fat oxidation, but these processes do not sterilise food.
pictures.caption: Airtight sealing, vacuum packaging and nitrogen flushing are different processes.

title: Vacuum Packaging, Airtight Containers and Nitrogen Flushing
